t.4.15.1: Then Vālī, who was in his inner apartments and could not bear his brother, heard that roar of the great-souled Sugrīva.
t.4.15.2: But on hearing his roar, which made all beings tremble, his intoxication vanished in an instant, and a great fury came upon him.
t.4.15.3: But Vālī, his limbs suffused with rage and glowing like the twilight sun, at once lost his radiance, like the sun seized by eclipse.
t.4.15.4: But Vālin, terrible with his fangs and like a blazing fire in his wrath, shines like a lake whose lotuses have risen up together with their stalks.
t.4.15.5: Hearing that unbearable sound, the monkey then rushed forth with great speed, as if splitting the earth with the stamping of his feet.
t.4.15.6: But Tārā, embracing him out of love and showing her deep affection, frightened and agitated, spoke these words, which held the promise of a good outcome.
t.4.15.7: O hero, rightly cast off this anger that has come upon you like the rushing current of a river, just as one who has risen from his bed at daybreak casts aside a garland already enjoyed.
t.4.15.8: Your going out so hastily does not please me at all. Listen, I shall tell you the reason for which you are being held back.
t.4.15.9: He who earlier rushed at you in anger now challenges you to battle, though when he sallied forth before, he was driven back by you and, being beaten, fled in all directions.
t.4.15.11: Such is the pride and the resolve of him who roars, and such the fury of his roaring, that this can be no trifling cause.
t.4.15.10: That he, who was driven off by you and badly beaten, should come here and challenge you again seems to awaken a suspicion in me.
t.4.15.12: I do not think that Sugrīva has come here without an ally; he has secured a firm ally, and it is relying on him that he roars like this.
t.4.15.13: By nature the vānara Sugrīva is both skillful and wise; he will not go along with one whose valor has not been tested.
t.4.15.14: O hero, I have already heard the words of Prince Aṅgada as he was relating them; now I shall tell you words that are for your good.
t.4.15.15: For your brother has a renowned ally, harsh in battle: Rāma, crusher of enemy forces, risen up like the fire at the end of an age.
t.4.15.16: He is a sheltering tree for the virtuous, the supreme refuge of those in distress, the sanctuary of the afflicted, and the sole abode of glory.
t.4.15.17: Endowed with knowledge and wisdom, devoted to his father's command, he is a great mine of virtues, as the lord of mountains is of minerals.
t.4.15.18: Therefore it is not fitting for you to be at enmity with that great-souled Rāma, who is invincible and immeasurable in the deeds of battle.
t.4.15.19: O hero, I shall tell you something, and I do not wish to find fault with you. Let it be heard and let it indeed be done: I shall tell you what is good for you.
t.4.15.20: Quickly and properly consecrate Sugrīva as heir apparent. Do not wage war, O hero, O king, with your more powerful brother.
t.4.15.21: Indeed, I consider it fitting for you to cast hostility far away and to make friendship with Rāma and affectionate concord with Sugrīva.
t.4.15.22: For this monkey, your younger brother, deserves to be cherished by you. Whether he stays there or here, he is in every way your own kinsman.
t.4.15.23: If what is pleasing to me is to be done by you, and if you know me to be your well-wisher, then, being earnestly entreated, carry out my good counsel.
